principle: Mix every sound by how relevant it is to the player
why: Sound effects play almost constantly, so each one needs a deliberate loudness, flashiness and discernibility. Judging only by the physical size of an action gives the wrong result; what matters is a sound's importance to the game and to the player character. Match-deciding events and direct feedback come first, ambience last.
how_to_apply: List every sound and rank it by relevance, then set volumes in that order. Smash's order, loudest first: KO; hits given or taken, and perfect shields; special-move activations and voices, with explosions between hits and specials and louder the bigger they are; dodges, shield blocks and ledge grabs; attack swings without impact and dashes; landings; jumps; walking; ambience lowest of all. Within a tier, scale by strength. Balance voices carefully, because clear speech cuts through everything. When voices or channels are limited, decide in advance which part yields.
anti_pattern: Volume set by how big the action looks. Ambience or chatter masking gameplay sounds. Every sound equally loud.
example: Smash's KO sound is the loudest because it is crucial to push and pull and decides the match; Link's quiet footsteps versus his quiet sword swing pose the question of which comes first.
review_question: Is the loudest sound at any moment the one that matters most to the player right then?
keywords: mixing mix priority volume loudness relevance hierarchy sound-effects sfx balance

principle: Make impact sounds hit instantly and clear out fast
why: Players need a reaction to their attack right away, so an impact sound must never feel late. Echo makes a sound feel stronger, but in fast battles with four or eight players, overlapping tails make it impossible to tell where each sound starts and everything gets buried in a sea of noise. Hence his policy: strong attack, light reverb.
how_to_apply: Shape hit sounds with a short attack that reaches a strong level almost immediately (not literally starting at peak volume). Trim reverb tails. Cut rapid jab sounds to the shortest length that still reads as consecutive hits. Time heavy hits so the main body of the sound plays during hitstop and is over when action resumes. Review in the busiest mix, not one sound at a time. Make sure the punch survives speakers that drop bass, and that the playback chain isn't delaying it.
anti_pattern: Impact sounds that swell in late. Long echoing tails that sound great solo and turn the mix to noise. Reviewing hits only in isolation.
example: Smash impact waveforms: loud at the start with a short tail, revised from the sound team's pre-check versions; jab sounds pared down; strong-hit sounds timed to finish inside hitstop; impact sounds arriving late through home theater systems.
review_question: In the busiest scene, can you hear exactly when each hit lands, and is its sound finished before the next one starts?
keywords: impact hit-sounds attack envelope transient reverb tail hitstop latency punch sfx combat mix

principle: Treat audio as essential, never as bolt-on polish
why: He can't think of a single masterpiece with bad audio, though masterpieces with bad graphics, or even without coherent game essence, exist. When people remember a game they loved, its music and sound effects are often the first things that come to mind; audio is what hits you right in the heart. Even old games with nothing but simple noise-based effects had well-constructed audio.
how_to_apply: Schedule and budget music and sound alongside graphics from the start. List audio changes for every character or major asset at kickoff, as you do for art and moves. Construct every sound deliberately, even with limited technology. Use what new hardware makes possible to do something the old one couldn't. Tie presentation to music, for example by starting play as a stage's musical intro ends. Benchmark against the sounds you remember from games you loved.
anti_pattern: Leaving audio until the end. Assuming players won't notice.
example: Kirby's Dream Land's Sound Test, stages that begin right after their musical intro and Kirby's victory dance; Melee's streamed, orchestral tracks; the 70 to 100 planned changes per Smash Ultimate fighter, covering audio as well as graphics and moves.
review_question: If players remembered one sound or melody from our game, what would it be?
keywords: audio-quality importance music sound-design memorable budget schedule priority masterpiece

principle: Answer every input and every feat with sound
why: If a player acts and the game gives no reaction, it feels lacking. Swing, dash and footstep sounds exist as feedback for button presses, and landings are a reaction. Items and progress don't specifically say 'well done', so praise has to be added on purpose, and it works best when it heightens what the player already feels.
how_to_apply: Give every accepted press a clear signal, sound included. Keep input-feedback sounds audible even at low mix priority. Add crowd reactions tied to skill: cheers for big launches and KOs, a subtle 'oh!' for near-misses like a barely caught ledge. Let spectators clap along to victory music. Consider vibration matched to the frequency of impact sounds.
anti_pattern: Silent actions or menus. Praise limited to item drops. One generic 'Good!' for everything.
example: The Smash crowd's gasp when someone barely grabs a ledge; Kirby Air Ride's spectators clapping along to the dance music; Sakurai's own HD Rumble experiment matching vibration to impact sounds.
review_question: Is there any press, success or close call in the game that makes no sound at all?
keywords: feedback input-feedback responsiveness praise crowd cheers reactions near-miss rumble haptics

principle: Exaggerate action sounds; keep material and ambient sounds realistic
why: Real punches would sound like a bunch of slaps, and fighting games are nothing like real fighting; forget that and you drift away from the game essence you want. Realistic sounds have their own power: they give meaning to things simple graphics can't show, such as the weight of wood and stone. Ambience works best fairly realistic, even in cartoony games. But the more realistic the visuals, the stranger exaggerated sounds feel.
how_to_apply: Decide each sound category's job: selling impact (exaggerate) or conveying material, weight and place (keep realistic). A/B real recorded hits against exaggerated ones. Give simple-graphics games distinct material sounds. Layer realistic ambience even under cartoon art. Set the overall exaggeration level against how realistic your visuals are, and unify audio across mixed sources the way you unify art.
anti_pattern: Literal realism in combat audio. Cartoon sounds over photoreal visuals. Simple visuals backed by generic sounds that carry no material information.
example: Street Fighter II's wildly fake impacts, in the tradition of Showa-era film sound; Minecraft's thunks that help you picture what you're building; hits that sound painful as a form of imitation that enriches a game's information.
review_question: For each sound, is its job impact or information, and does its realism level fit both that job and the visuals?
keywords: exaggeration realism fiction non-fiction foley impact material sounds stylization sound-design

principle: Never leave dead silence; keep ambience quiet but alive
why: Ambient sounds are the least important and take the lowest priority, so they must never cover the sounds that matter. But if the player stops for a second and hears dead silence, there's no atmosphere, and games should make players feel they've entered another world, especially in first-person or over-the-shoulder views. A handful of well-chosen sounds can imply a whole world beyond the screen, and players with good speakers notice whether ambience is well made.
how_to_apply: Mix ambience at the lowest priority. Stop in every area and just listen, and add layers wherever it's silent. Give realistic visuals a soundscape (wind in leaves, feet on dirt, clinking armor), each layer at an appropriate level. In simulations, call a few simple off-screen sounds to suggest activity. Check ambience on good speakers. Put extra effort in for first-person and over-the-shoulder games. Keep music from standing out too much over detailed visuals.
anti_pattern: Silence whenever the action stops. Ambience so busy it buries key effects. Foreground chiptune-style music fighting dense, realistic visuals.
example: Smash stages played with the volume raised to reveal their many quiet ambient sounds; a train simulator's clattering doors and shuffling feet; NES-style music over modern games sounding noisy and 'off'.
review_question: If you put the controller down anywhere in the game, what do you hear?
keywords: ambience ambient-sound atmosphere immersion soundscape room-tone background-sound silence world-building

principle: Finalize sound on cheap TVs and several setups, not studio speakers
why: Most players hear the game through small TV speakers that lose low frequencies, so impacts hit less hard and details tuned in a pristine studio can become inaudible. Each listening environment reveals different problems. A fixed reference keeps standards steady; change your headphones mid-project and it's hard to stay consistent with everything checked before.
how_to_apply: Compare important sounds on headphones, PC speakers and an inexpensive TV before approving them. Watch sounds whose punch lives in the bass. Check good speakers for ambience quality. Keep the same reference gear all project. Don't tune so hard for weak speakers that you lose your creative vision. Check audio latency separately from video. Check every audio feature you rely on exists on each hardware variant you ship.
anti_pattern: Signing off on big studio speakers alone. Swapping reference headphones mid-project. Over-correcting until the mix loses its character.
example: His order of checks: headphones, PC speakers, then most importantly a cheap TV; the Switch's built-in speakers sit low on the list because they're already clear and many handheld players play muted.
review_question: Has every key sound been approved on a cheap TV as well as on headphones and PC speakers?
keywords: monitoring speakers tv-speakers headphones listening-test reference mastering low-frequency bass latency hardware

principle: Never make sound the only carrier of critical information
why: Many players play handhelds with the sound off, or somewhere they can't hear the game; a player who can't hear the audio has no idea when enemies are firing. The reverse holds too: audio and vibration cues can carry information to players who can't easily see it.
how_to_apply: Give every audio warning a visual tell players can react to, and treat sound as a reinforcing layer for critical events. Where it helps, offer audio and vibration cues as accessibility options, such as a sound near a spot you can jump to or an item you can pick up, and combat cues.
anti_pattern: Incoming attacks signaled only by sound. Key information delivered only in voice.
example: A crossover host who couldn't hear the game audio and so couldn't tell when enemies were firing; Punch-Out!!'s yellow eyes as a visual dodge cue; traversal and combat audio cues and vibration cues in a modern accessibility menu.
review_question: Muted, can a player still see every warning? And does sound add the information it should for players who rely on it?
keywords: accessibility redundancy muted deaf hard-of-hearing visual-cue audio-cue telegraph warnings captions haptics

principle: Build the soundtrack on a few memorable themes
why: He thinks too many songs get produced for a single game, and admits he's guilty of it too. Huge soundtracks are harder to remember and harder to get excited about. A song has more impact if people can remember its melody, so restraint and arrangement beat sheer volume.
how_to_apply: Write one main theme early and plan where its arrangements appear across the game. Cut or merge tracks that have no melody players could hum. When arranging, keep the main melody intact so that humming the arrangement is humming the original.
anti_pattern: A new, unrelated song for every scene. A soundtrack nobody can hum.
example: His habit of writing a main theme and arranging it throughout the game; the Star Wars theme as the reason a familiar melody shouldn't change from film to film.
review_question: Can a playtester hum the main theme after a session?
keywords: music soundtrack main-theme leitmotif melody arrangement memorable hummable restraint

principle: Match music tempo and mood to the action and the player's feeling
why: Some tempos fit a game's content and others don't. Even among similar fighting games, the right tempo depends on the speed of the action, and scenes within one game need their own tempos and rhythms. Songs work best when they complement how the player is feeling. Tempo is everyone's concern, not just the composer's.
how_to_apply: Count BPM by clapping along (one clap per second is 60 BPM, two is 120) and note a target per scene. For fast battles, start from roughly 130 to 170 BPM, with near-200 tracks as rare exceptions. Set tempo by your game's actual speed, not its genre. Write one line per scene on what the player should feel and check the music supports it. Consider tying tempo to game state if you can afford it.
anti_pattern: One tempo for the whole game. A genre-default tempo that doesn't fit the actual pace. Music that works against the player's mood.
example: Smash battle arrangements at a little over 120 BPM, 130 to 170 on average, a few near 200; the first Dragon Quest's dungeon music slowing the deeper you go.
review_question: For each scene, what is the music's BPM, and what is the player supposed to feel there?
keywords: tempo bpm music mood pacing rhythm adaptive-music scene-music feeling

principle: Brief sound work with concrete roles, shared references and examples
why: Audio has no physical form and you can't approximate it with your voice, so vague requests fail, especially in text over remote work. Not everyone knows every sound, even a real one. A reference track is a fast way to set direction, but composers often can't tell which parts to keep. A director may know what he wants and still lack the musical language to say it.
how_to_apply: Decide what feedback and feeling each sound must give before requesting it. Describe its role concretely ('strong attack'). Compare only to universally known sounds ('a jet engine') and link an example for anything specific. Use onomatopoeia only as an extra clue next to a concrete description. Give one reference track with what to keep and what not to copy. Route musical feedback through a sound director. Agree on terms like 'main melody' by playing the reference together.
anti_pattern: Emails asking only for more 'clang' or 'boom'. 'Make it like this' with no notes. Assuming everyone knows the sound in your head.
example: God Hand's 'Gene's Rock-a-Bye', requested in the style of The Ventures but without their famous riff; the Athena arrangement that kept coming back opposite to his notes because he and the musicians meant different melodies by 'main melody'.
review_question: Could the sound designer tell from your request alone what the sound is for and what to borrow from the reference?
keywords: audio-direction sound-feedback brief reference-track communication onomatopoeia sound-director composer commission

principle: Approve the sound that serves the game, not the one in your head
why: It's not just about creating 'good' sounds but finding the right type of sounds for your game. Delivered sounds may differ from what you imagined and sometimes sound even better. A reference can save work or create more, and fixating on it closes off other possibilities. Having a clear idea of the goal from the start is what makes this judgment possible.
how_to_apply: Judge drafts by whether they fit the game and the scene, not by how closely they match your idea or the reference. List two or three other directions before locking a reference. Balance multi-environment fixes against your creative vision. If an existing song fits the theme exactly, consider licensing it as-is.
anti_pattern: Rejecting a fitting sound only because it differs from your mental image. Every draft a cheap imitation of one reference. Sounds that impress in isolation but are wrong for the mix.
example: Sakurai approving sounds quite different from his original idea; Ore no Shikabane wo Koete Yuke licensing the song 'Hana' because blooming and wilting flowers fit a family cursed with a two-year lifespan.
review_question: Are we judging this sound by whether it serves the game, or by whether it matches what we pictured?
keywords: approval judgment flexibility fit references fixation licensing creative-vision review

principle: Shape music structure around gameplay timing
why: Music and play share a timeline: a match countdown, a typical match length, a segment of known length, or a fight whose length varies. When the structure fits, music can be timed to the exact beats and moods of a scene; when it doesn't, intros get talked over and climaxes land at the wrong moment.
how_to_apply: Brief composers with gameplay-driven rules: an intro that covers any start countdown (or music that starts after it), big dynamic shifts for a dynamic game, a build to a climax at the end, a length that fits the typical match with only a little loop, and a loop point before or after the intro. Use fixed-length segments to sync music to beats. Plan cue points where music waits for or follows variable-length events. Start play as a stage's musical intro ends.
anti_pattern: Loops that restart mid-match. Music cues that ignore when the action actually happens.
example: Smash's '3, 2, 1, GO!' intro rule and its two-minute (two and a half in Ultimate) target length; Kid Icarus: Uprising's air battles of known length with music timed to their beats; the PRESS START orchestra following his live mid-boss kill.
review_question: Where do the countdown, the climax and the loop point fall relative to how long a typical play segment lasts?
keywords: music-structure loop intro countdown match-length cue-points sync adaptive-music beats composition brief

principle: Ground characters with audible, varied, material-aware footsteps and landings
why: In many 3D games footsteps are barely audible, which makes characters feel like they're hovering instead of walking. Landing is a reaction and deserves more presence than the jump. Believable sounds feel best, and one sample repeated over and over sounds mechanical.
how_to_apply: Make footsteps clearly audible. Give each character unique footsteps. Match landing and walking sounds to footwear or costume and to the floor material. Record several variations of repeated sounds and rotate them. Make landings louder than jumps.
anti_pattern: Near-silent footsteps. One footstep sample for every surface. The same sample on every step.
example: Cloud's landing sounds differ by costume; every Smash fighter got unique footsteps.
review_question: Walk a character across every floor type: do the steps sound grounded, varied and right for the surface?
keywords: footsteps landing foley surfaces materials variation randomization movement-sounds grounding

principle: Script every vocalization; keep battle voices short, sparse and non-competing
why: Recording a fighter's voice takes about an hour, but the result goes straight into the game and players hear it constantly, so writing and directing dialogue carries a lot of responsibility. Anything not in the script won't get recorded. Long lines or excessive chatter in battle draw too much attention and break immersion, and clear speech cuts through other sounds.
how_to_apply: List every grunt and line (attacks, jumps, damage reactions, special and super moves, reveal lines). Bring reference audio from the original game and prefer the original or current series actor. Keep combat lines short and infrequent, and check how loud or feral voices overlap. Brief and warm up actors before they enter the booth. Record banter-heavy casts together when schedules allow. Budget heavy editing time after recording. Where you can, deliver dialogue as voice during play so players needn't stop.
anti_pattern: Missing grunts. Constant battle chatter. Voices that compete. No editing time. Patching lines recorded in a different room.
example: Smash's one-hour sessions per fighter (two at most with reveal or story lines); extra care for Bowser's and Donkey Kong's overlapping voices; Kid Icarus: Uprising's cast recorded together for banter; his own channel voiceover re-recorded only as a last resort because a new room sounded different.
review_question: Is every vocalization scripted, and does any voice line overstay its welcome or clash with another during play?
keywords: voice voice-acting vo dialogue barks grunts recording script casting editing localization chatter

principle: When arranging beloved music, treat the original as players heard it as right
why: Listeners come for one familiar song out of a great many, so an arrangement that turns out totally different disappoints. The song you hear when playing the original is what's right, even when it strays from musical convention, quirks and hardware-driven structure included, and arrangers must not detract from each player's memory of it. Recreated sounds should match how they came out of the original hardware.
how_to_apply: Keep the main melody intact. Decide which melody is 'main' by what players heard and remember from play. Preserve odd sections. Mirror structure the hardware forced, such as an instrumental where the original lost its vocals. Keep separate language versions distinct. Recreate how a sound came out of the original cabinet, not just the raw file. Review for mistranscriptions of the original score.
anti_pattern: 'Correcting' quirks. Rewriting a melody because it feels old-fashioned to you. Copying the raw audio file when players remember the cabinet.
example: Athena's section that hits on-beats the first time and off-beats the second, reproduced in Smash; Psycho Soldier's English arrangement going verse, instrumental, verse because the original switched to the internal audio processor after verse one; Ryu's impact sounds tuned to sound like the arcade cabinet.
review_question: Would a longtime fan humming our arrangement be humming the original?
keywords: arrangement remix cover nostalgia original fidelity melody licensed-music fan-expectations

principle: When voices or channels are scarce, plan what yields and fit timbre to role
why: On the Famicom, music and sound effects shared the same five channels, so part of the music often had to cut out whenever an effect played, and composers gave each role the waveform that suited it. The same budgeting applies wherever polyphony, memory or storage is limited, and features can differ between hardware versions.
how_to_apply: Decide in advance which music part drops when a sound effect needs a voice. Give crisp tones to melodies, mellow tones to bass and noise-like sounds to hits and explosions. Test compression on big audio sets early, before cutting content. Check every hardware variant or region supports the audio features you rely on, or provide a fallback.
anti_pattern: Letting effects steal the melody at random. Discovering missing audio features on a regional version.
example: The Famicom's two pulse, one triangle, one noise and one DPCM channel; Super Mario Bros. 3's timpani sample; NES cartridges losing expansion audio; Smash Ultimate's music library compressed into a quarter of the space it took in Smash for.
review_question: When every voice is busy, what drops out, and was that our choice?
keywords: polyphony channels voice-stealing chiptune famicom nes timbre compression memory hardware-limits

principle: Let players reach and choose the music they love
why: Each generation has its own version of a series, and so its own music, which made one song per world feel wasteful. Some players also want to enjoy the music from the start rather than earn it as a reward.
how_to_apply: Where your game celebrates many sources, offer several tracks per world and let players choose. Don't lock music many players want behind progression. Give options such as menu-music frequency.
anti_pattern: Locking favorite music behind long progression.
example: Brawl's My Music; Smash cutting back on music used as rewards; adjustable menu-music frequency after beating Ultimate.
review_question: Can players hear the music they came for without grinding for it?
keywords: music-player jukebox unlocks my-music options player-choice rewards

principle: Showcase game music live with the performance at the center
why: He believes live music can stir emotions you can't find elsewhere. In a concert the performance is the point, and video after video distracts from it. Live, one-time stakes are what make a gameplay performance thrilling.
how_to_apply: Gather far more candidate songs than you have slots and narrow them down by listening together. Use game footage only occasionally. Size each edition so it fits beside development work. If gameplay joins the performance, keep real stakes and plan cue points for variable timing.
anti_pattern: Video after video during a concert.
example: PRESS START: ten annual concerts from 2006, 14 to 16 program pieces (about 60 songs counting medleys); his Intensity 9.0, zero-defense Kid Icarus air battle played live with the orchestra; Melee's orchestral tracks leading to those concerts.
review_question: In this showcase, is the audience's attention on the music?
keywords: concert orchestra live-performance showcase curation press-start events
